_comment: Guard-pin registry, read by harness/swe/guardpin.py (round 413, SWE-loop D). A pin is a CLAIM: 'if this call stopped doing its job, THIS named test would tell us.' The runner falsifies it — it applies the declared edit in a throwaway copy and requires the named test to go RED. Sites are located SYMBOLICALLY (path + func + target), never by line number: a line number rots silently and would have the tool confidently mutating whatever moved into its place, while a symbol that moved makes the pin `unlocatable` and loud. `keep_call: true` keeps the call running and its NAME in the source and discards only its VALUE, which is what tells a source-grep pin apart from a behavioural one; it is rejected as an `equivalent` edit on a bare call statement, where the value is discarded anyway. Add a pin whenever a round's knowledge file says 'and this test pins it' — that sentence is the claim this file exists to check.

pins.why: round 411's exemption gate, asked by the FIRST of its two doors. Neutering its answer to None makes every placeholder token a checkable claim again — the pre-411 behaviour of the other door.

the SECOND door — round 411's actual bug. The claimed guardian is a structural pin whose own docstring says it 'cannot prove the call is on the right path'; keep_call=true is the edit that tests that sentence.
GP02's twin with the call TEXT removed. Same site, same test; the only difference is whether the identifier survives. Whatever the two verdicts are, their difference is the measurement.
round 349's fix: without this raise a campaign scores a suite that never ran, and scores it HIGH.
round 349's whitelist. False here restores the pre-349 rule that every non-zero exit code is a kill, including the ones that mean the suite never ran.
the gate campaign.py's five run_mutant call sites forgot. Its claimed guardian is structural — it counts occurrences in the file — so this pin asks whether removing the call is enough to trip it.

round 412's input guard. A power floor computed from N <= 0 is a number with no record behind it. `expect_in_failure` added after the first run: the test DID go red, but with `ZeroDivisionError: division by zero` from inside power_floor rather than with `DID NOT RAISE`. Red by crash is not the same evidence as red by the assertion the test is named for.

round 412's `untestable` verdict. False is 0 numerically, so p_best * n_tested <= bar always holds and NOTHING is ever untestable — the pre-412 world, where a unit with no power was graded `coincidence`.

the `power` block round 412 put in every attribution report. None here means the report still has the key and no number behind it. `expect_in_failure` added after the first run: under the edit this test dies with `TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not subscriptable` inside channel_sweep and never evaluates ANY of its four assertions. It is red, and it is not red about n_testable_units -- round 412's shape, one layer out.
v0.3's tail marking on the NAMED-fn branch. Without it no call is ever in tail position, so the tail-loop optimisation silently stops applying.
the SAME call on the ANONYMOUS-fn branch (v0.14.10). Two doors, one behaviour, one named guardian — the round-411 shape, asked before it becomes a bug.

GP11 widened from one file to the whole whence fast tier. Round 413's own killer tests are DESELECTED here on purpose: the question this pin answers is the pre-fix one — did any of the ~1000 fast-tier tests notice this call being deleted BEFORE round 413 added a test for it — and leaving them in would have the round grading its own homework.

GP11's killer. Round 413 measured the survivor (nothing in test_v03.py noticed), built the differential (peak_depth 1 -> 50, tail_calls 300 -> 0 for a let-bound anonymous fn, named fn unchanged) and turned it into this test. The pin is what keeps that true.
